title: Adam and Eve
lead: The first man and woman in Genesis 2–5. Their names mean "Human" and "Life." The New Testament sets Adam beside Christ (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45), and how to understand them historically is much debated today.

sections.h: Adam and Eve across the Bible
sections.b: Outside Genesis 1–5, the Old Testament names Adam only in 1 Chronicles 1:1 (and possibly Hosea 6:7, "they, like Adam, overstepped the covenant," though it may mean "at Adam," a place). Jewish writings of the time of Jesus reflect on him often: "O Adam, what have you done?" (2 Esdras 7:118). The New Testament makes Adam the head of humanity: Luke traces Jesus' line to "Adam, son of God" (Luke 3:38), Paul says death came through one man and life through another (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49), and he cites Adam and Eve on marriage and worship (1 Corinthians 11:8–12; 1 Timothy 2:13–14). Eve is named in 2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Timothy 2:13. Views on whether they were the only first pair, a historical couple chosen from a larger population, archetypes, or figures for humanity are summarized in the note at Genesis 2:7.
